questions.question: Explain why food spoils and describe how the main methods of preservation work by denying spoilage organisms what they need.
questions.expected_answer: Food spoils because living things consume it: bacteria and moulds from the air, hands and surfaces multiply if they find moisture, warmth and usually air, producing smells, slime and sometimes toxins; yeasts ferment sugars; insects such as weevils lay eggs in grain; rodents eat and foul stored food. Each spoiler needs certain conditions, and preservation removes one or more: drying removes moisture; cooling slows organisms and freezing stops them; sealing excludes air, insects and animals; salt and sugar draw water out of organisms; acid prevents most bacteria growing; heat kills organisms and sealing keeps new ones out; smoke both dries food and coats it with growth-inhibiting chemicals. Preservation matters as much as production because a harvest must last until the next and post-harvest losses can reach a third of a crop.

questions.question: Describe indigenous and modern methods of storing grain and compare them, stating the common cause of failure.
questions.expected_answer: Both rest on keeping grain dry, cool, sealed and off the ground. Indigenous methods in southern Africa dried grain in sun and in the smoke of the cooking hut, which also deterred insects; stored it in woven baskets raised on stilts under a thatched cap, with stones or collars to stop rats, the raised floor keeping grain off damp ground; sealed it in pits dug in dry ground, lined with grass or dung plaster and capped with clay so that insects suffocated and the earth kept it cool; and kept it in lidded, plastered clay pots. Modern methods use steel or concrete silos filled with grain dried to about 12 percent moisture, ventilated by fans, sealed against pests and fumigated, as well as sealed plastic bags on farms and lidded buckets at home. Indigenous methods use local materials, need no power and suit small quantities; modern ones handle vast quantities with precise moisture control at higher cost. Both fail when moisture enters, through a leaking cap, a cracked wall or an open lid, after which mould grows and can make the grain unsafe.

questions.question: Explain how pickling preserves food, distinguishing pickling with vinegar from pickling by fermentation, and state the rules for successful pickling.
questions.expected_answer: Pickling keeps food in an environment too acidic for most spoilage bacteria to grow. With vinegar, vegetables are packed in clean jars and covered with vinegar, a solution of about 5 percent acetic acid, often with salt, sugar and spices; the acid soaks in and the whole jar becomes inhospitable, as with pickled onions, gherkins, beetroot and the vinegar component of atchar. By fermentation, vegetables are packed in brine and sealed from air; salt-tolerant lactic acid bacteria naturally present feed on the vegetable's sugars and produce lactic acid until the brine is too sour for anything else to grow, as in sauerkraut, kimchi, fermented African vegetables and sour maize and sorghum drinks such as mageu. Rules: the food must be fully covered by the liquid, since anything above it moulds; the jar must be clean and sealed; the acid must be strong enough, undiluted vinegar or a fermentation run until properly sour; salt assists; and once opened the jar is kept cool.
